Volume and timbre can be controlled by pressing the chains with the palm of the non-dominant hand and by the way the instrument is turned and swung; striking the chains directly gives a tapping sound, but very little volume. If the beads are pressed before turning, there are fewer short grace notes, but the sound is duller and more solid. Against the maraca its typical sound depends more on friction between beads and ridges; against the African bead-net gourd type, agbe or cabaça, the metal version makes a metallic friction sound from the ridged cylinder. 卡巴薩搖響器常見於拉丁爵士，尤其巴薩諾瓦編制中，以金屬珠鏈摩擦圓柱產生細密節奏；: The cabasa is common in Latin jazz, especially in bossa nova line-ups, where the metal chains rub against the cylinder to make a fine-grained rhythm; in Latin American dance music it appears in the bead-net gourd form. Pop music also uses it as a rhythmic accompaniment, and wind bands and orchestral works take it up from time to time. The African originals, agbe and cabaça, belong to the same class of shaker, and it is often used in music therapy, since a small movement of the hand is enough to sound it.
卡巴薩搖響器與非洲及南美洲相關。非洲原始版本稱 agbe，以曬乾葫蘆外覆珠網發聲: The cabasa is connected with Africa and South America. The African original, called agbe, sounds from a dried gourd covered with a bead net; instruments of the same kind also appear in Latin American dance music. The modern metal version was created by Martin Cohen, with metal bead chains wrapped around a cylinder; it is common in Latin jazz and bossa nova and has entered pop and orchestral scoring. There is also a pedal variant, in which a spring-loaded pedal controls the chains and extends the ways of playing.

Begin with this, then practise holding the handle in one hand and swinging it up and down so that chains and ridges strike each other; striking the chains directly is less used, because it is quiet. A single note in the score often contains several short grace notes, and an exact written value is hard to achieve; you can press the beads first and soften the sound with the gesture, but the sound becomes duller. Because only a tiny hand movement is needed to sound it, it also suits beginners and therapeutic practice.

The African original has a dried gourd as its body, covered with a bead net. The pedal variant has a scraper at the edge of the pedal that scrapes the chains, but the source does not state what the scraper is made of. The cabasa, also called the iron sand rattle, is a percussion instrument and an idiophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 112.13. The modern type has ridged metal sheet around a cylinder with several metal bead chains, and a wooden or plastic handle at the lower end; the African version has a dried gourd covered with a bead net. The player holds the handle in one hand and lays the other palm on the chains, then turns the handle so that the chains rub the ridges and make a dense cha-cha sound; the instrument can also be swung up and down or the chains struck directly. It is common in Latin jazz, bossa nova, pop music and orchestral works, and it is also used in music therapy.
